doc_summary: Beth Barnes (METR) discusses how to build capability and alignment evaluations by working backwards from threat models, with attention to elicitation, task validity, sandbagging, and buffers. She stresses that evidence is only meaningful if tasks truly capture the real-world activity and that sloppy setups yield misleading results.

items.claim: Prefers working backwards from a concrete threat model to realistic activities and then to runnable tasks over generic benchmarks or abstract-ability tests, because benchmarks poorly predict real-world danger and saturate quickly.
items.quote: we’re trying to more work backwards from the threat model, and that might end up getting distilled into something that is more like an ML benchmark where it’s looking for some particular cognitive ability, but it’s working backwards from these threat models

items.claim: A task is a weak test if converting a real-world activity into a codeable, repeatable task loses real-world properties or introduces distributional shift, so one should ask whether the task is systematically easier or harder than the real thing.
items.quote: And that’s going to lose various real-world properties once you actually make one specific task and you can’t have the model actually doing criminal things.

items.claim: Distrusts measurements where an unnoticed flaw in the setup (misleading instructions, environment quirks like bot detection, task ambiguity) makes a result reflect the setup rather than the model.
items.quote: But then the code was running on a data center so it got bot-detected by something else in a way that it hadn’t done. It just could be all these random ways you thought you’d de-risked something and then it’s like, oh, it’s actually impossible for this stupid reason.

items.claim: Notes that refusal or sandbagging-like behaviour is more likely when a task looks nefarious or far from what labs train on, so a setup that reads as nefarious or unusual changes model behaviour versus a natural assistant-style task.
items.quote: An innocuous sort of common task in an assistant format where someone’s asking you to help them debug some code or something like that, you’d expect that the model basically should be doing its best on that.

items.claim: Prefers doing elicitation on a dev set and evaluating on a held-out test set over task-specific prompt tuning, because narrow elicitation puts the cognitive work and the answer into the setup.
items.quote: So the way we think you should actually do this is you do all your elicitation against a dev set and then you evaluate on a separate test set so it’s fair.

items.claim: In a setup, patch capabilities likely to be fixed soon (e.g., a human acting as the browsing tool) instead of letting every task fail for the same artefact, because uniform failures give no information about the next bottleneck.
items.quote: You don’t want to be in the situation where all of your tasks are failing for the same reason, that you think is a thing that might change quickly, because then you’re just not getting any information

items.claim: Prefers starting alignment evaluation with basic, observable misbehaviour tests like obvious reward hacking over galaxy-brain deceptive-alignment scenarios, because the basics may be skipped and are more tractable.
items.quote: I feel like people sometimes jump to kind of galaxy-brain deceptive alignment stuff and I worry that we won’t do the basics of just being like, well, is the model just obviously reward hacking or something?

items.claim: To probe misalignment, measure how much hand-holding is needed to get a model to take nefarious opportunities and how nearby such behaviour is, and test whether training removes planted bad tendencies via model organisms.
items.quote: seeing exactly how much hand-holding do you need to get the model to start doing nefarious things and reward hacking and taking advantage of opportunities.

items.claim: Treats task-validity problems as analogous to work tests: a failure may reflect luck, misunderstanding of the prompt, or an unreasonable-but-reasonable interpretation, so single outcomes are weak evidence.
items.quote: Or they misunderstood something at the start that was a reasonable misunderstanding that you didn’t see because you’d written the question, so you thought it was obvious that it pointed you in this direction or something.

items.claim: Prefers claiming bounded, caveated conclusions (soft upper bounds with stated assumptions, research collaborations not audits) over overclaiming, and notes casual demos get over-read.
items.quote: We weren’t thinking of that as a significant thing at all when we did it, but somehow everyone was very excited about it. That was more just us messing around

items.claim: Names open problems: alignment and control evals once capabilities are present, plus scary demos and model organisms of sandbagging.
items.quote: We also would love to be doing more stuff on alignment and control evals and thinking of, once you’re no longer at the point where the model doesn’t even have these capabilities, then what do you do?
